title.en: Effort and Destiny Argue the Case (Liezi)
title.zh: 力謂命曰：若之功奚若我哉（列子力命篇）

region.en: The debate between human striving and fate (symbolic pin: Song, Henan, China)
region.zh: 力命之辯（象徵定位：宋，今河南）

texts.period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book VI (Effort and Destiny)

summary.en: Effort claims power over length of life, success, rank, and wealth; Destiny answers with the catalogue of misallotments — P'êng Tsu's wisdom did not exceed Yao and Shun's, yet he lived eight hundred years; Yen Yüan's ability was not inferior, yet he died at thirty-two; Po I and Shu Ch'i starved at Shou-yang while Chi Shih waxed rich. When the way is straight, I push on; when it is crooked, I let be.
summary.zh: 力謂命曰：若之功奚若我哉？命曰：彭祖之智不出堯舜之上，而壽八百；顏淵之才不出眾人之下，而壽十八——窮聖而達逆，賤賢而貴愚。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon. Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: EFFORT said to Destiny: "Your achievements are not equal to mine." "Pray what do you achieve in the working of things," replied Destiny, "that you would compare yourself with me?" "Why," said Effort, "the length of man's life, his measure of success, his rank, and his wealth, are all things which I have the power to determine." To this, Destiny made reply: "P'êng Tsu's wisdom did not exceed that of Yao and Shun, yet he lived to the age of eight hundred. Yen Yüan's ability was not inferior to that of the average man, yet he died at the early age of thirty-two. The virtue of Confucius was not less than that of the feudal princes, yet he was reduced to sore straits between Ch'en and Ts'ai.

Chi Cha would not accept the overlordship of Wu, while T'ien Hêng usurped sole power in Ch'i. Po I and Shu Ch'i starved to death at Shou-yang, while Chi Shih waxed rich at Chan-ch'in. If these results were compassed by your efforts, how is it that you allotted long life to P'êng Tsu and an untimely death to Yen Yüan; that you awarded discomfiture to the sage and success to the impious, humiliation to the wise man and high honours to the fool, poverty to the good and wealth to the wicked?" ... "When the way is straight, I push on; when it is crooked, I let be. Old age and early death, failure and success, high rank and humble station, riches and poverty -- all these come naturally and of themselves. Of their ultimate causes, I am ignorant; how could it be otherwise?"

title.en: Chi Liang's Deathbed and the Three Doctors (Liezi)
title.zh: 季梁之疾，三醫並進（列子力命篇）

region.en: Yang Chu's friend's sick-room (symbolic pin: Kaifeng, Henan, China)
region.zh: 楊朱友人病榻（象徵定位：河南開封）

texts.period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book VI (Effort and Destiny)

summary.en: Yang Chu chants to his weeping friend's sons that over his destiny man has no control. Three doctors diagnose in turn: the origin is traceable to disordered appetites — you are only one of the common ruck, says Chi Liang; it is incurable — you are a good doctor; lastly Dr. Lu: it was already fore-ordained in the mind of Providence when you were endowed with this bodily form at birth — you are a heaven-born physician indeed! Not long after, his illness disappeared of itself.
summary.zh: 楊朱歌曰：天其弗識，人胡能覺？——汝疾非由天，非由人，亦非鬼神；命之所制也。季梁曰：天醫也！

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon. Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: Yang Chu then chanted the following words: "How should men possess the knowledge which God Himself has not? Over his destiny man has no control, and can look for no help from God. You and I know this for truth, but our knowledge is not shared by sorcerers and quacks." The sons, however, did not understand, and finally called in three physicians, Dr. Chiao, Dr. Yü and Dr. Lu.

Lastly, Dr. Lu said: "Your illness is attributable neither to God, nor to man, nor to the agency of spirits. It was already fore-ordained in the mind of Providence when you were endowed with this bodily form at birth. What possible good can herbs and drugs do you?" "You are a heaven-born physician indeed!" cried Chi Liang; and he sent him away laden with presents. Not long after, his illness disappeared of itself.

title.en: Duke Ching Weeps on the Ox-Mountain and Yen Tzŭ Smiles (Liezi)
title.zh: 齊景公遊於牛山，北臨其國城而流涕（列子力命篇）

region.en: The Ox-mountain north of Linzi (Niushan, Shandong, China)

texts.period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book VI (Effort and Destiny)

summary.en: Duke Ching of Ch'i, gazing from the Ox-mountain at his lovely kingdom, weeps that some day he must die and leave it; two fawning ministers weep too. Yen Tzŭ smiles: if the worthy ruler were to remain in perpetual possession, Duke T'ai and Duke Huan would still be exercising their sway — condemned to a hard life on earth, you would have had no time for brooding over death. The Duke fines himself two cups of wine.
summary.zh: 齊景公遊於牛山，北臨其國城而流涕曰：美哉國乎！若何滂滂去此而死乎！晏子獨拊心大笑。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon. Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: Duke Ching of Ch'i was travelling across the northern flank of the Ox-mountain in the direction of the capital. Gazing at the view before him, he burst into a flood of tears, exclaiming: "What a lovely scene! How verdant and luxuriantly wooded! To think that some day I must die and leave my kingdom, passing away like running water! If only there were no such thing as death, nothing should induce me to stir from this spot." Two of the Ministers in attendance on the Duke, taking their cue from him, also began to weep.

Yen Tzu replied: "If the worthy ruler were to remain in perpetual possession of his realm, Duke T'ai and Duke Huan would still be exercising their sway. If the bold ruler were to remain in perpetual possession, Duke Chuang and Duke Ling would still be ruling the land. But if all these rulers were now in possession, where would your Highness be? Why, standing in the furrowed fields, clad in coir cape and hat! ... And are you alone going to weep and lament over this order of things? That is unmanly. It was the sight of these two objects -- an unmanly prince and his fawning attendants -- that was affording me food for laughter just now."

title.en: Tung-men Wu Does Not Mourn His Son (Liezi)
title.zh: 魏有東門吳者，其子死而不憂（列子力命篇）

region.en: The State of Wei (Anyang region, Henan, China)

texts.period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book VI (Effort and Destiny)

summary.en: Tung-men Wu of Wei testifies no grief when his son dies. There was a time when I had no son, he answers his house-steward; during the whole period that elapsed before my son was born, I never had occasion to grieve. Now that my son is dead, I am only in the same condition as I was before I had a son — what reason have I, then, to mourn?
summary.zh: 魏有東門吳者，其子死而不憂。其室家曰：子之愛子，天下無有；今子死不憂，何也？東門吳曰：吾嘗無子，無子之時不憂。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon; paralleled in Zhuangzi's drum-on-basin mourning scenes. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: There was once a man, Tung-men Wu of Wei, who when his son died testified no grief. His house-steward said to him: "The love you bore your son could hardly be equalled by that of any other parent. Why, then, do you not mourn for him now that he is dead?" "There was a time," replied Tung-men Wu, "when I had no son. During the whole period that elapsed before my son was born, I never had occasion to grieve. Now that my son is dead, I am only in the same condition as I was before I had a son. What reason have I, then, to mourn?"

title.en: Do You Know Why You Hit the Target? (Liezi)
title.zh: 列子學射中矣，請於關尹子（列子說符篇）

region.en: Kuan Yin Tzŭ's archery-ground (symbolic pin: Hangu Pass, Lingbao, Henan, China)
region.zh: 關尹子之射場（象徵定位：河南靈寶函谷關）

texts.period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book VII (Causality)

summary.en: Lieh Tzŭ learns archery and, able to hit the target, asks Kuan Yin Tzŭ's opinion. Do you know why you hit the target? No. Then you are not good enough yet. Three years of practice later: Yes, I do — hold that knowledge fast and do not let it slip.
summary.zh: 列子學射中矣，請於關尹子。尹子曰：子知子之所以中乎？對曰：弗知也——三年，又以報關尹子。曰：可矣，守而勿失也。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon. Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: Lieh Tzü learned archery and, when he was able to hit the target, he asked the opinion of Kuan Yin Tzü on his shooting. "Do you know why you hit the target?" said Kuan Yin Tzü. "No, I do not," was the reply. "Then you are not good enough yet," rejoined Kuan Yin Tzü. Lieh Tzü withdrew and practised for three years, after which he again presented himself. Kuan Yin Tzu asked, as before: "Do you know why you hit the target?" "Yes," said Lieh Tzü, "I do." "In that case, all is well. Hold that knowledge fast, and do not let it slip."

title.en: Three Years to Carve a Mulberry Leaf in Jade (Liezi)
title.zh: 宋人以玉為楮葉（列子說符篇）

texts.period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book VII (Causality)

summary.en: A man of Sung carves a mulberry leaf out of jade for his prince; it takes three years, and imitates Nature so exquisitely that it cannot be distinguished from real leaves in a heap. Lieh Tzŭ hears of it: if it took the Creator three years to make a single leaf, there would be very few trees with leaves on them — the Sage will rely not so much on human science and skill as on the evolution of Tao.
summary.zh: 宋人有為其君以玉為楮葉者，三年而成；列子曰：使天地三年而成一葉，則物之有葉者寡矣。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon. Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: There was once a man in Sung who carved a mulberry leaf out of jade for his prince. It took three years to complete, and it imitated Nature so exquisitely in its down, its glossiness, and its general configuration from tip to stem, that, if placed in a heap of real mulberry leaves, it could not be distinguished from them. This man was subsequently pensioned by the Sung State as a reward for his skill. Lieh Tzu, hearing of it, said: "If it took the Creator three years to make a single leaf, there would be very few trees with leaves on them. The Sage will rely not so much on human science and skill as on the evolution of Tao."

title.en: The Two Sons of Mr. Shih and Mr. Meng (Liezi)
title.zh: 魯施氏二子，孟氏同業（列子說符篇）

region.en: The courts of Ch'in and Wei (Xianyang and Anyang, China)

texts.period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book VII (Causality)

summary.en: Mr. Shih's two sons, scholar and soldier, rise through Ch'i and Ch'u; his poor neighbour Mr. Meng's sons apply the same formula and come to grief — castrated in Ch'in, feet cut off in Wei. Success consists in hitting off the right moment, answers Mr. Shih; nothing in the ordering of this world is either at all times right or at all times wrong.
summary.zh: 魯施氏有二子，其一好學，其一好兵；孟氏同業而不同得——秦王宮刑之，衛侯刖之。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon. Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: Mr. Shih of Lu had two sons, one of whom was a scholar and the other a soldier. The former found in his accomplishments the means of ingratiating himself with the Marquis of Ch'i, who engaged him as tutor to the young princes. The other brother proceeded to Ch'u, and won favour with the King of that State by his military talents. The King was so well pleased that he installed him at the head of his troops. Thus both of them succeeded in enriching their family and shedding lustre on their kinsfolk.

The eldest son immediately set off for Ch'in, hoping that his moral culture would recommend him to the King of that State. But the King said: "At the present moment all the feudal princes are struggling to outbid one another in power, and the great essential is to keep up a large army. If I tried to govern my State on the lines of altruism and righteousness, ruin and annihilation would be the outcome." So saying, he had the unfortunate man castrated, and turned him away. The second son, meanwhile, had gone to Wei ... so, without more ado, he cut off his feet and sent him back to Lu.

Mr. Shih, however, said: "Success consists in hitting off the right moment, while missing it means failure. Your method was identical with ours, only the result was different. That is not due to any flaw in the action itself, but simply because it was not well timed. Nothing, in the ordering of this world, is either at all times right or at all times wrong. What formerly passed current may nowadays be rejected; what is now rejected may by and by come into use again."

title.en: The Duke's Laugh: the Silkworm-Tender and the Escorted Wife (Liezi)
title.zh: 晉文公將伐衛，公子鉏仰天而笑（列子說符篇）

region.en: The army of Chin on the march (Houma, Shanxi, China)

texts.period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book VII (Causality)

summary.en: Duke Wên of Chin marches to attack the Duke of Wei; Tzŭ Ch'u throws his head back and laughs — recalling the neighbour who escorted his wife to her family and stopped to court a silkworm-tending woman, only to find his own wife receiving the attentions of an admirer. The Duke saw the point and turned home — before an invading force had already crossed his northern frontier.
summary.zh: 晉文公出，將伐衛；公子鉏仰天而笑——郊有蠶婦——見其妻之受非望之遇也。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon. Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: Duke Wen of Chin put an army into the field with the intention of attacking the Duke of Wei, whereat Tzŭ Ch'u threw his head back and laughed aloud. On being asked the reason of his behaviour, he replied: "I was thinking of the experience of a neighbour of mine, who was escorting his wife on a visit to her own family. On the way, he came across a woman tending silk worms, who attracted him greatly, and he fell into conversation with her. Happening to look up, what should he see but his own wife also receiving the attentions of an admirer! It was the recollection of this incident that made me laugh." The Duke saw the point, and forthwith turned home with his army. Before he got back, an invading force had already crossed his northern frontier!

title.en: Ch'i Yung, Who Could Tell a Robber by His Face (Liezi)
title.zh: 晉之郗雍能視盜（列子說符篇）

region.en: The robber-infested Chin State (Houma, Shanxi, China)

texts.period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book VII (Causality)

summary.en: In the robber-infested Chin State, Ch'i Yung could tell a robber by his face and read his inmost thoughts; the Marquis delights in him — until the robbers band together and murder him. Wen Tzŭ of Chao has foretold it, quoting the Chou proverb: search not the ocean-depths for fish — and prescribes promoting the worthy to office instead; all the robbers flee to Ch'in.
summary.zh: 晉侯曰：吾有一人，逐盜而獲之。文子曰：以察伺盜，盜不盡矣——周諺有言：察見淵魚者不祥。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon. Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: In the Chin State, which was infested with robbers, there lived a certain Ch'i Yung, who was able to tell a robber by his face; by examining the expression of his eyes he could read his inmost thoughts. The Marquis of Chin employed him in the inspection of hundreds and thousands of robbers, and he never missed a single one. The Marquis expressed his delight to Wen Tzu of Chao, saying: "I have a man who, single-handed, is ridding my whole State of robbers." Wen Tzu replied: "If your Highness relies on a detective for catching robbers, you will never get rid of them. And what is more, Ch'i Yung is certain sooner or later to meet with a violent end."

Meanwhile, a band of robbers were plotting together. "Ch'i Yung," they said, "is the enemy who is trying to exterminate us." So one day they stole upon him in a body and murdered him. ... "In Chou," replied Wen Tzu, "we have a proverb: 'Search not the ocean-depths for fish: calamity comes upon those who pry into hidden mysteries.' If you want to be quit of robbers, the best thing your Highness can do is to promote the worthy to office." The Marquis then appointed Sui Hui to be Prime Minister, and all the robbers fled to the Ch'in State.

title.en: Chiu-fang Kao and the Superlative Horse (Liezi)
title.zh: 秦穆公九方皋相馬（列子說符篇）

region.en: The court of Duke Mu of Ch'in (Xianyang, Shaanxi, China)
region.zh: 秦穆公之廷（今陝西咸陽）

texts.period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book VII (Causality)

summary.en: Po Lo recommends the fuel-and-vegetable hawker Chiu-fang Kao, who returns after three months with a steed at Sha-ch'iu — a dun-coloured mare, he says, though it turns out a coal-black stallion. Much displeased, the Duke summons Po Lo, who heaves a sigh of satisfaction: what Kao keeps in view is the spiritual mechanism — in making sure of the essential, he forgets the homely details. When the horse arrived, it turned out indeed to be a superlative horse.
summary.zh: 秦穆公謂伯樂：子之年長矣——九方皋相馬：牝而驪——得其精而忘其粗，在其內而忘其外。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon; the judge-of-horses topos paralleled in Zhuangzi ch. 24. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: "You are now advanced in years. Is there any member of your family whom I could employ to look for horses in your stead?" Po Lo replied: "A good horse can be picked out by its general build and appearance. But the superlative horse -- one that raises no dust and leaves no tracks -- is something evanescent and fleeting, elusive as thin air. The talent of my sons lies on a lower plane altogether: they can tell a good horse when they see one, but they cannot tell a superlative horse. I have a friend, however, one Chiu-fang Kao, a hawker of fuel and vegetables, who in things appertaining to horses is nowise my inferior."

However, on some one being sent to fetch it, the animal turned out to be a coal-black stallion! Much displeased, the Duke sent for Po Lo. "That friend of yours," he said, "whom I commissioned to look for a horse, has made a nice mess of it. Why, he cannot even distinguish a beast's colour or sex!" Po Lo heaved a sigh of satisfaction. "Has he really got as far as that?" he cried. "Ah, then he is worth a thousand of me put together. What Kao keeps in view is the spiritual mechanism. In making sure of the essential, he forgets the homely details; intent on the inward qualities, he loses sight of the external. So clever a judge of horses is Kao, that he has it in him to judge something better than horses." When the horse arrived, it turned out indeed to be a superlative horse.

title.en: The Dead Rat Dropped by the Kite (Liezi)
title.zh: 白頷之鴞腐鼠（列子說符篇）

region.en: The rich man's balcony over the high road (symbolic pin: Kaifeng, Henan, China)
region.zh: 梁富人北宮之上（象徵定位：河南開封）

texts.period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book VII (Causality)

summary.en: A lucky throw of the dice evokes a burst of merriment from Mr. Yü's gambling party above the main road; precisely at that moment a kite sailing overhead drops the carcass of a rat among the young gallants below, who take it for an insult and exterminate every member of the family. Pride and extravagance lead to calamity and ruin in more ways than one.
summary.zh: 虞氏富樂無比——梁上有鴞，墮其腐鼠於中——虞氏之患以驕奢故也。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon. Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: Mr. Yü was a wealthy man of the Liang State. It was his custom to have banquets served, to the accompaniment of music, in a high upper hall overlooking the main road; there he and his friends would sit drinking their wine and amusing themselves with bouts of gambling. One day, a party of young gallants happened to pass along the road. In the chamber above, play was going on as usual, and a lucky throw of the dice, which resulted in the capture of both fishes, evoked a loud burst of merriment from the players.

Precisely at that moment, it happened that a kite which was sailing overhead dropped the carcass of a rat in the midst of the company outside. The young men held an angry consultation on the spot: "This Mr. Yü has been enjoying his wealth for many a long day, and has always treated his neighbours in the most arrogant spirit. And now, although we have never offended him, he insults us with this dead rat. ... Let us summon up our utmost resolution, and combine with one accord to wipe him and his family out of existence!" The whole party signified their agreement, and when the evening of the appointed day had come, they collected, fully armed for the attack, and exterminated every member of the family.

title.en: The Honest Man Who Could Not Eat a Robber's Gruel (Liezi)
title.zh: 東方有士曰爰旌目，食於盜者（列子說符篇）

region.en: The hungered road of the east (symbolic pin: Linyi, Shandong, China)
region.zh: 東方之塗（象徵定位：山東臨沂）

texts.period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book VII (Causality)

summary.en: Yüan Ching Mu, overcome by hunger on the road, is fed with a bowl of rice-gruel by the robber Ch'iu of Hu-fu; after three mouthfuls he learns his benefactor's name, cries: I am an honest man and cannot eat your food — and clutches the ground with both hands, retching and coughing to bring it up again.
summary.zh: 爰旌目曰：嘻！汝非盜邪？胡為而食我？吾義不食子之食也。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon. Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: In the east of China there was a man named Yuan Ching Mu, who set off on a journey but was overcome by hunger on the way. A certain robber from Hu-fu, of the name of Ch'iu, saw him lying there, and fetched a bowl of rice-gruel in order to feed him. After swallowing three mouthfuls, Yuan Ching Mu opened his eyes and murmured, "Who are you?" "I am a native of Hu-fu, and my name is Ch'iu." "Oh misery!" cried Yuan Ching Mu, "are not you the robber Ch'iu? What are you feeding me for? I am an honest man and cannot eat your food." So saying, he clutched the ground with both hands, and began retching and coughing in order to bring it up again.
